title: OneLake Architecture: Namespace, Shortcuts, Storage, and Security
purpose: Show how OneLake's single tenant-wide namespace, open Delta storage format, shortcut virtualization, and layered security model combine into one governed data surface that every Fabric engine reads without copying data.
accessibleSummary: An architecture diagram starting from the one-per-tenant OneLake namespace, which contains workspaces and items whose tabular data lands as open Delta Parquet files. From there, two branches: item data can be read directly by multiple compute engines (Spark, T-SQL, Analysis Services) with no per-engine copy, or it can be extended virtually through OneLake shortcuts that reference data inside or outside the tenant without moving it. Shortcuts split into internal shortcuts, which pass through the calling user's own identity, and external or delegated shortcuts, which authorize through a bound connection identity and compute access as the intersection of what that identity and the end user are each permitted to see. A layered OneLake security model (control plane, data plane, hierarchical roles) governs every read regardless of path, and a warning node calls out the antipattern of standing up separate physical lakes per team instead of using workspaces and shortcuts.
longDescription: This is an architecture diagram of OneLake as the storage substrate of Microsoft Fabric. It begins at the tenant boundary, where exactly one OneLake is provisioned and virtualized as a single ADLS Gen2-compatible namespace. Workspaces and items live inside that namespace, and any item's tabular data is automatically persisted as open Delta Parquet, regardless of which engine wrote it. From that single-copy Delta layer, the diagram branches two ways: direct multi-engine consumption, where Spark, T-SQL, and Analysis Services all read the identical physical bytes with no duplication; and shortcut virtualization, where OneLake shortcuts reference data elsewhere without copying it. Shortcuts further split into internal shortcuts (pass-through identity, calling user must independently hold read permission at the target) and external/delegated shortcuts (authorization bound to a connection identity, with delegated access computed as an intersection of the delegated identity's and the end user's permissions). A dedicated OneLake security model node shows the two-plane (control/data) hierarchical permission system that governs every one of these read paths uniformly. A warning node captures the documented antipattern of standing up separate physical data lakes per business group instead of using OneLake's workspace-and-shortcut model, which reintroduces the duplication and operational overhead OneLake exists to eliminate.

nodes.label: One OneLake per tenant
nodes.summary: Exactly one OneLake is provisioned per Fabric tenant; none can be added or removed.
nodes.detail: Every Microsoft Fabric tenant is provisioned with exactly one OneLake. Tenants cannot create additional OneLake instances or delete the existing one, and no separate storage resources need to be provisioned or managed — it exists as soon as the tenant does. This is the architectural starting point: there is no per-team or per-project OneLake to stand up, only workspaces inside the single tenant-wide one.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because there is only ever one OneLake, every downstream architectural decision in this diagram — workspaces, shortcuts, security roles — operates inside one namespace rather than across independently provisioned storage accounts that would need their own governance.

evidence.note: Every Fabric tenant is provisioned with exactly one OneLake; tenants cannot create additional instances or delete the existing one, and no separate storage resources need to be provisioned or managed.

inputs: A newly created Microsoft Fabric tenant, mapped one-to-one with a Microsoft Entra tenant
processing: Fabric provisions OneLake automatically at tenant creation
OneLake is layered on Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and exposes ADLS Gen2 APIs/SDKs
The tenant maps to the root of one continuous file-system namespace
outputs: A single, always-present OneLake ready to hold workspaces and items with no manual storage provisioning
drill.example: A new organization signs up for Fabric; before any workspace is created, OneLake already exists as the tenant's storage root — the first workspace created simply becomes a container inside it, with no separate storage-account setup step.
controls: None at the OneLake-existence level — this is not a configurable choice
Tenant-level security, compliance, and data-management policy set once, applying to everything that later lands in OneLake
failureModes: Assuming a new business unit needs its own OneLake or storage account, and provisioning one unnecessarily
Treating OneLake as optional infrastructure to configure rather than the default, always-on substrate

nodes.label: Workspace / item namespace
nodes.summary: Tenant, workspaces, and items form one continuous ADLS-virtualized namespace.
nodes.detail: OneLake's addressing model virtualizes the whole tenant as one giant ADLS storage account: each Fabric workspace surfaces as a container in that account, and each data item (lakehouse, warehouse, eventhouse, and so on) surfaces as a folder inside its workspace container. Every path is unique across the whole tenant, so a Spark job and a T-SQL query referencing the same item point at the exact same bytes.
nodes.whyItMatters: This addressing scheme is what makes internal shortcuts and cross-engine access work without translation — every item has one canonical path, so nothing needs to be re-resolved or copied to be reached from a different engine or workspace.

evidence.note: OneLake's addressing model virtualizes the whole tenant as one giant ADLS storage account: each workspace surfaces as a container, and each data item surfaces as a folder inside its workspace container.

inputs: Workspaces created under the tenant, each attached to a capacity in a region
Items created inside those workspaces (lakehouse, warehouse, eventhouse, KQL database, etc.)
processing: Fabric assigns each workspace a container path under the tenant's OneLake account
Fabric assigns each item a folder path inside its workspace container
The resulting ABFSS-style path becomes the single canonical address for that item's data
outputs: A globally unique, ADLS-compatible path per item, addressable identically from Spark, T-SQL, Power BI, and external ADLS-aware tools
drill.example: A lakehouse named 'sales' in workspace 'analytics-prod' resolves to one fixed OneLake path; a Spark notebook, a T-SQL query against the SQL analytics endpoint, and an external Databricks job referencing the same abfss:// path all read the identical underlying files.
controls: Workspace-to-capacity and workspace-to-region assignment at creation time
Item naming, which becomes part of the permanent addressable path
failureModes: Renaming an item and assuming external tools referencing the old path will still resolve
Treating workspace/item paths as arbitrary strings rather than the actual addressing contract other engines depend on

nodes.label: Delta Parquet, one copy
nodes.summary: All Fabric item data lands in OneLake as open Delta Parquet, regardless of writing engine.
nodes.detail: All Fabric data items, including lakehouses and warehouses, automatically persist their tabular data in OneLake using the open Delta Parquet format, regardless of which engine wrote the data. This one-copy design lets multiple Fabric engines — T-SQL, Apache Spark, Analysis Services, and others — operate over the exact same physical Delta Parquet data, so teams do not duplicate datasets per engine or get locked into whichever engine first loaded it.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the foundational guarantee the rest of the architecture depends on: because storage format is uniform and open, every consumption path and every shortcut in this diagram reaches the same physical bytes instead of a per-engine copy that could drift.

evidence.note: All Fabric data items automatically persist their tabular data in OneLake using the open Delta Parquet format, regardless of which engine wrote the data; this one-copy design lets multiple engines operate over the same physical data without duplication or lock-in.

inputs: Writes from any Fabric engine (Spark job, warehouse T-SQL insert, pipeline copy activity, mirroring change feed)
processing: Engine writes Parquet data files plus a Delta transaction log entry
OneLake registers the resulting table/folder under the item's canonical path
No format conversion step exists between engines
outputs: A single physical copy of Delta Parquet data, immediately queryable by every engine that can read Delta
drill.example: A Spark job writes a gold sales table; without any export or ETL step, the warehouse's T-SQL engine and a Power BI Direct Lake model both read that exact same Delta table the moment the Spark write commits.
controls: Choice of writing engine (does not affect the resulting open format)
V-Order and compaction settings that shape the physical Parquet layout without changing logical data
failureModes: Building an export/copy pipeline between engines out of habit, recreating the duplication OneLake's one-copy model is meant to eliminate
Assuming a non-Delta write (raw CSV/Parquet dropped into Files/) gets the same auto-registration and multi-engine guarantees — it does not

nodes.label: Multi-engine consumption
nodes.summary: Spark, T-SQL, and Analysis Services all query the same Delta files with no per-engine copy.
nodes.detail: Because OneLake speaks the standard ADLS Gen2 API and SDK surface, and every engine writes the same Delta Parquet format, Spark notebooks, the SQL analytics endpoint or warehouse T-SQL engine, and Analysis Services (via Direct Lake) can all query one physical copy of an item's data concurrently, with no shortcut-specific or engine-specific logic required.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the direct payoff of the single-namespace, single-format design: teams pick the engine that fits their skillset or workload without forking the data, and a change made by one engine is immediately visible to the others.

evidence.note: The one-copy design lets multiple Fabric engines — T-SQL, Apache Spark, Analysis Services, and others — operate over the same physical Delta Parquet data, so teams do not duplicate datasets per engine.

inputs: A Delta table already resident in OneLake under an item's canonical path
processing: Spark reads/writes via Spark SQL or the DataFrame API
T-SQL reads via the SQL analytics endpoint (lakehouse/mirrored/SQL database) or full warehouse engine
Analysis Services reads directly in Direct Lake mode for a Power BI semantic model, with no import refresh
outputs: Three concurrently valid query surfaces over the same physical data, each reflecting the latest committed state
drill.example: A data engineer writes a new partition with Spark at 9:00am; by 9:01am an analyst's Direct Lake report and a separate T-SQL ad hoc query against the SQL analytics endpoint both reflect the new rows, with no refresh or export triggered in between.
controls: Which engine a given workload uses is a skills/workload choice, not a data-availability constraint
Direct Lake vs Import vs DirectQuery mode selection on the semantic model layer
failureModes: Assuming an engine change requires a data migration, when it is usually just a different query surface over the same files
Building custom sync jobs between engines that are already reading the same physical data

nodes.label: OneLake shortcuts
nodes.summary: Symbolic-link-style references that virtualize data inside or outside the tenant with no copy.
nodes.detail: A OneLake shortcut is an object that points from a shortcut path to a target path in another storage location; it behaves like a symbolic link, so deleting the shortcut leaves the target untouched, while moving, renaming, or deleting the target can break the shortcut. Shortcuts are transparent to consumers — through the OneLake API they look like ordinary folders, so any engine queries them with no shortcut-specific logic.
nodes.whyItMatters: Shortcuts extend the one-copy model beyond a single item: instead of copying data to unify it, teams reference it in place, which is what lets OneLake unify data across workspaces, tenants, and even non-Fabric clouds without an ETL step.

evidence.note: A OneLake shortcut is an object that points from a shortcut path to a target path in another storage location; it behaves like a symbolic link, and is transparent to consumers — Spark, SQL, RTI, and non-Fabric ADLS-compatible tools all query shortcut data with no shortcut-specific logic.

inputs: A target path: another item in the same or a different workspace/tenant, or an external store (ADLS Gen2, S3, GCS, Dataverse)
processing: Create the shortcut interactively in the Fabric portal or programmatically via the OneLake shortcuts REST API
Fabric registers the shortcut as a folder reference at the chosen path
Any Delta-format target under Tables/ auto-registers as a queryable table
outputs: A folder that reads and queries exactly like native data, with zero bytes duplicated
drill.example: An analytics lakehouse creates a shortcut into a supply-chain team's lakehouse Tables/inventory folder; a Spark notebook in the analytics workspace reads Tables/inventory_shortcut as though it were a local table, with no copy job involved.
controls: Shortcut target selection and naming (no spaces — Delta format disallows them in table names)
Whether the shortcut is created at the top level of Tables/ (auto-discovered) or nested in Files/ (not auto-discovered)
failureModes: Naming a table shortcut with a space, which the Delta format rejects, silently preventing table auto-registration
Deleting or renaming a shortcut target without updating dependents, breaking every shortcut that points at it

nodes.label: Internal shortcuts (pass-through)
nodes.summary: Reference other Fabric items; access authorized as the calling user's own identity.
nodes.detail: Internal OneLake shortcuts can target data in other Fabric items — lakehouses, warehouses, KQL databases, SQL databases, mirrored databases, semantic models — across items and workspaces, and access through them is authorized with the calling user's own identity, which must independently hold read permission at the target.
nodes.whyItMatters: Pass-through identity means the source item's owner never has to provision access on behalf of consumers — each caller's own permissions decide what they can see, keeping authorization consistent regardless of which shortcut path they used to reach the data.

evidence.note: Internal OneLake shortcuts can target data in other Fabric items across items and workspaces, and access through them is authorized with the calling user's own identity, which must hold read permission at the target.

For pass-through shortcuts, OneLake security cannot be additionally configured on the shortcut path itself; access is evaluated only at the target, so the data owner retains full, exclusive control regardless of which shortcut path is used.

inputs: A shortcut pointing at another Fabric item's table or folder
The calling user's own Entra ID identity and their OneLake security grants at the target
processing: OneLake evaluates the caller's identity against the target item's permissions, not the shortcut path's
If the caller lacks read permission at the target, the read fails even though the shortcut itself exists
outputs: A read authorized exactly as if the caller queried the target item directly
drill.example: Two teams share an analytics workspace with a shortcut into a finance lakehouse; an analyst without read permission on the finance lakehouse still cannot query the shortcut, even though it appears in their own workspace's Tables folder.
controls: Grant/revoke read permission at the target item, which immediately propagates to every internal shortcut pointing at it
failureModes: Assuming DirectLake-over-SQL or T-SQL delegated-identity mode preserves per-user passthrough through a shortcut — those specific modes actually authorize as the item owner, not the caller

nodes.label: External / delegated shortcuts
nodes.summary: Reach non-Fabric stores or cross-tenant data via a bound connection identity, not the caller's.
nodes.detail: ADLS and S3 shortcuts delegate authorization to a cloud connection bound at shortcut creation; binding is a privileged operation. Delegated OneLake Shortcuts extend this pattern to OneLake-to-OneLake and cross-tenant sharing: access flows through one configured connection identity (organizational account, service principal, or workspace identity) instead of each individual signed-in user's identity, and delegation is optional — shortcuts default to pass-through unless explicitly delegated at creation.
nodes.whyItMatters: Delegation is what lets a shortcut scale to broad or cross-tenant distribution: instead of provisioning every downstream consumer at the source, one connection identity is scoped once, and consuming teams manage their own users behind it.

evidence.note: ADLS and S3 shortcuts delegate authorization to a cloud connection bound at shortcut creation; binding is a privileged operation, so a user without permission on the connection cannot create new shortcuts that use it.

Delegated OneLake Shortcuts add a second shortcut authentication mode where access flows through one configured connection identity instead of each signed-in user's identity; the identity can be an organizational account, service principal, or workspace identity, and delegation is optional per shortcut.
Delegated shortcuts support cross-tenant sharing: one Fabric tenant can shortcut to OneLake data in a different organization's tenant, authenticating with an identity from that other tenant.

inputs: An external target (ADLS Gen2, S3, GCS, Dataverse) or a cross-tenant/cross-workspace Fabric target
A bound connection identity: cloud connection, org account, service principal, or workspace identity
processing: Bind a connection/identity at shortcut creation (privileged operation)
OneLake authorizes reads through that bound identity rather than the caller's own
For delegated OneLake shortcuts specifically, the effective access is the intersection of the delegated identity's permissions and the end user's own OneLake security grant
outputs: A shortcut usable by many downstream consumers without provisioning each one individually at the source
drill.example: A central sales lakehouse creates a delegated shortcut into an EMEA regional workspace using service principal spn-emea-reader, scoped via OneLake security to EMEA rows only; EMEA analysts see the intersection of what spn-emea-reader can read and what their own OneLake role grants — never more than the service principal's own scope.
controls: Scope the delegated identity's own permissions narrowly at the source — this is what actually caps downstream exposure
Choose pass-through vs. delegated deliberately at creation time; switching later requires deleting and recreating the shortcut
failureModes: Treating the delegated identity as a blank check and relying only on the consuming workspace's own permissions, without also constraining the delegated identity at the source
Assuming a mode switch (pass-through to delegated) is an in-place setting — it requires delete and recreate

nodes.label: OneLake security model
nodes.summary: Two-plane, hierarchical permissions govern every read path uniformly, shortcut or not.
nodes.detail: OneLake security operates on two planes: control plane permissions decide what users can do (create, manage, share items), while data plane permissions — the OneLake security model — decide what data users can read. Permissions follow the storage hierarchy of workspace, item, and folder, inheriting from the parent by default. A OneLake security role composes scope (tables/folders), permission, member users, and optional row/column constraints.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single policy layer that every consumption path in this diagram — direct engine query, internal shortcut, or delegated shortcut — is ultimately evaluated against, which is what keeps governance consistent no matter how data is reached.

evidence.note: OneLake security operates on two planes: control plane permissions decide what users can do, while data plane permissions (the OneLake security model) decide what data users can read; control plane grants often confer data access by default.

A OneLake security role is composed of the data (tables or folders) in scope, the permission granted, the member users, and optional constraints that carve out specific rows or columns, enabling table, folder, row-level, and column-level security.

inputs: Custom OneLake security role definitions scoped to specific tables/folders
processing: Evaluate the caller's workspace role first — Admin/Member/Contributor can read/write OneLake data outright; Viewer needs an explicit OneLake security role
Apply item-level sharing scope if the caller reached the item via sharing rather than workspace membership
Apply any custom OneLake security role constraints (row/column scope) on top
outputs: An effective read/write decision per request, consistent whether the request came via direct query, internal shortcut, or delegated shortcut
drill.example: A Viewer with no explicit OneLake role queries a lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint and is denied, despite being able to see the item exists in the workspace; granting them ReadData or a scoped OneLake security role resolves it without changing their workspace role.
controls: Scope custom OneLake security roles narrowly to specific tables/folders rather than relying on the broad built-in DefaultReader role
Choose the correct item-sharing grant (Read vs ReadData vs ReadAll) for the access pattern actually needed
failureModes: Relying on OneLake security roles to restrict workspace Admins, Members, or Contributors — those roles bypass OneLake security entirely and can read/write all item data
Leaving the built-in DefaultReader role unedited, granting any ReadAll-permitted user access to all lakehouse data

nodes.label: Antipattern: siloed physical lakes
nodes.summary: Standing up separate physical lakes per team recreates the duplication OneLake eliminates.
nodes.detail: Standing up separate physical data lakes per business group, a common pre-OneLake practice, is an antipattern in Fabric because it recreates resource-management overhead and data duplication that the single tenant-wide OneLake with workspaces and shortcuts is designed to eliminate. The correct pattern for organizational separation is workspaces plus shortcuts, not a second storage account.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the most common architectural regression teams migrating into Fabric make — bringing over the old per-team-lake habit defeats the single biggest structural advantage OneLake offers.

evidence.note: Standing up separate physical data lakes per business group is an antipattern in Fabric because it recreates the resource-management overhead and data duplication that the single tenant-wide OneLake with workspaces and shortcuts is designed to eliminate.

inputs: A migration or new-project plan that defaults to 'give each team its own storage account/lake'
processing: Team requests isolated storage instead of a workspace inside the tenant's one OneLake
A second physical lake is provisioned, requiring its own governance, backup, and security configuration
Data that could have been a shortcut is instead copied or pipeline-synced into the new lake
outputs: Duplicate physical copies of data that drift out of sync, plus doubled operational overhead
drill.example: A newly onboarded business unit is given its own ADLS Gen2 storage account 'for isolation' instead of a Fabric workspace with scoped OneLake security roles; six months later its data has diverged from the source system because nobody maintained the sync pipeline between the two.
controls: Default new team onboarding to a workspace inside the existing OneLake, not a new storage account
Use workspace-level and OneLake-security-role scoping to achieve organizational separation instead of physical isolation
failureModes: Data duplication and drift between the siloed lake and the source of truth
Doubled security, backup, and compliance surface area with no corresponding benefit

edges.label: if teams bypass workspaces for separate lakes

walkthrough.title: Start: one OneLake, always present
walkthrough.explanation: Every Fabric tenant gets exactly one OneLake automatically — no provisioning step, no second instance possible.

walkthrough.title: Tenant, workspaces, items — one namespace
walkthrough.explanation: OneLake virtualizes the entire tenant as one ADLS-compatible account, with workspaces as containers and items as folders inside them, giving every item one canonical, engine-neutral path.

walkthrough.title: Item data lands as open Delta Parquet
walkthrough.explanation: Regardless of which engine writes it, tabular data becomes Delta Parquet — the one-copy foundation every other node in this diagram builds on.

walkthrough.title: Branch: read directly with any engine
walkthrough.explanation: Spark, T-SQL, and Analysis Services (Direct Lake) all query the same physical files concurrently, with no per-engine copy.

walkthrough.title: Branch: reference data without copying it
walkthrough.explanation: OneLake shortcuts extend the one-copy model beyond a single item, virtualizing data from elsewhere in the tenant or outside it entirely.

walkthrough.title: Internal shortcuts pass through the caller's identity
walkthrough.explanation: A shortcut to another Fabric item authorizes as the calling user, who must independently hold read permission at the target.

walkthrough.title: External and delegated shortcuts use a bound identity
walkthrough.explanation: Shortcuts to external stores or across tenants authorize through a connection identity instead, with delegated access computed as an intersection of what that identity and the end user can each see.

walkthrough.title: One security model governs every path
walkthrough.explanation: Whether data is reached directly or through a shortcut, the same two-plane, hierarchical OneLake security model is what ultimately authorizes the read.

walkthrough.title: Warning: don't rebuild per-team lakes
walkthrough.explanation: Standing up a separate physical lake per team instead of using a workspace plus shortcuts recreates exactly the duplication and overhead OneLake was built to remove.
